stories.headline: Houthi drone strike on Riyadh's PIF tower injures 11, including two Indians
stories.dek: The Saudi-led coalition struck Hodeidah port on Wednesday after the Houthis threatened Jeddah and other Saudi Red Sea ports; India condemned the attack.
stories.summary: A Houthi strike on a tower in Riyadh's financial district on Tuesday injured 11 people, two of them Indians, Saudi authorities said. India condemned the attack, and the Saudi-led coalition later struck targets in Hodeidah, Saada and Amran.
body: A Houthi strike on a tower in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District injured 11 people on Tuesday, including two Indian nationals, Saudi Civil Defence said, and India's external affairs ministry condemned the attack on Wednesday.

Civil Defence described the incident as a "terrorist attack" by the Houthi militia. Those hurt were two Saudi citizens, two Indians, three Nepalese and four Egyptians. Saudi authorities did not name the tower, but shared an image of the Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower, according to The New York Times. Business Standard, citing Saudi authorities, said a Houthi drone struck the tallest tower in Riyadh.

The Houthis did not immediately confirm the attack, The New York Times reported. The group has repeatedly threatened the district and carried out at least two earlier strikes that damaged buildings there, the newspaper said. Hindustan Times reported that an attack on November 19 caused material damage to a tower and nearby buildings but no injuries.

The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia confirmed on X that two Indian nationals were injured. It said it was ascertaining details and would extend all possible assistance to the injured and their families. It also asked Indians in the kingdom to abide by local rules and regulations.

In its statement, the ministry of external affairs called for an immediate end to strikes. "We also reiterate our firm solidarity with the people and Government of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and reaffirm our unwavering support to the Kingdom in safeguarding its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the security and safety of its citizens and residents," it said.

On Wednesday, Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree said Jeddah and all other Saudi ports on the Red Sea coast would be targeted if Saudi Arabia carried out threats to attack the Yemeni port of Hodeidah. He urged port workers and people nearby to evacuate and asked shipping companies to withdraw their vessels.

After that statement, the Saudi-led coalition said it targeted operational capabilities at Hodeidah and destroyed a number of targets in the Yemeni governorates of Saada and Amran. The coalition had vowed a firm response to the Riyadh attack, Business Standard reported.
Hodeidah is the main entry point for food and other essential supplies to Houthi-controlled northern Yemen.
keyFacts: Eleven people were injured in Riyadh on Tuesday, November 24, according to Saudi Civil Defence.
The injured include two Saudis, two Indians, three Nepalese and four Egyptians.
An earlier strike on a Riyadh tower on November 19 caused damage but no injuries.
The coalition said it struck Hodeidah, Saada and Amran on Wednesday.
Houthis threaten Jeddah and other Saudi Red Sea ports if Hodeidah is attacked.
stories.background: Renewed fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has intensified since September, when the Houthis advanced towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping chokepoint at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. The Houthis have since stepped up strikes on Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities, while Saudi Arabia has increased airstrikes on Houthi targets in Yemen.
stories.whyItMatters: Foreign nationals, including Indians living in Saudi Arabia, have been injured, and the threat to Red Sea ports and shipping, and to Hodeidah's supply of food and aid, is growing.

perspectives.summary: Saudi Civil Defence called the Riyadh strike a terrorist attack by the Houthi militia. The coalition vowed a firm response and said it targeted Houthi capabilities at Hodeidah.

stories.headline: US set to announce new tariffs on India, China, EU and 13 other economies
stories.dek: The duties, expected as soon as this week after a probe into excess industrial capacity, would stack on levies imposed in July, according to reports citing sources.
stories.summary: The Trump administration is preparing to release findings of a Section 301 probe into excess industrial capacity in 16 trading partners, including India, with new duties expected, according to Reuters and the Wall Street Journal. Final rates have not been disclosed.
body: The Trump administration is poised to release the findings of a probe into alleged excess industrial capacity in 16 major trading partners, including India, with new import duties expected, Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing three people with knowledge of the matter.

The Wall Street Journal reported that US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer could announce the tariffs as soon as this week, though sources cautioned that the timing could change. The White House and the USTR's office did not respond to Reuters queries.

The probe was opened in March under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. It covers China, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Switzerland, Norway, Singapore, Bangladesh, Cambodia and the European Union.

Greer has said government subsidies and other support have created excess capacity in these economies, allowing their firms to sell cheaper goods in global markets and undermine US producers, the WSJ reported.

Final rates are unclear. One source told Reuters the duties would be tailored to each country, and that goods from Mexico and Norway were unlikely to face immediate levies. The WSJ said steel, aluminium and automobiles, already tariffed under a national security authority, are expected to be excluded.

The new duties would be added to those announced in July after a separate probe into forced-labour enforcement, which set rates of 10% to 12.5% on dozens of partners. India was first placed in the 12.5% bracket and later moved to 10%, Mint reported.

The White House is expected to honour tariff caps in finalised trade deals, Reuters reported, including 15% for the EU, Japan and South Korea and 19% for Malaysia. The 20% cap on China would hold if a trade truce expiring on January 10 is extended. The WSJ said India and Vietnam could face higher rates depending on their deals.

Ryan Majerus, a former Commerce Department trade official now at King & Spalding, said the administration could propose rates of 15% to 25% for countries deemed to have excess capacity. He said it could instead set lower rates with clauses that raise them over time unless countries cut excess production.

India and the US finalised the framework of an interim trade agreement in February, but talks restarted after the Supreme Court struck down the earlier emergency-law tariffs. New Delhi is seeking lower tariffs than competitors such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia. DW reported that a deal remains elusive.
keyFacts: The probe covers 16 economies, including India, China, Japan, South Korea and the European Union.
The USTR opened the Section 301 excess capacity investigation in March.
July forced-labour duties of 10% to 12.5% would remain, with the new levies stacked on top.
India faces a 10% duty from July; final new rates are not yet known.
The US-China trade truce is due to expire on January 10.
stories.background: The Supreme Court struck down Mr Trump's first batch of tariffs in February 2026. The administration has since used Section 301 investigations, launched in March, to rebuild them. India's rate was cut to 18% under an interim framework, and an additional 10% was imposed in July.
stories.whyItMatters: New duties on top of existing levies could raise the cost of Indian exports to the US and complicate negotiations over a bilateral trade agreement, in which India seeks lower tariffs than competitor nations.

stories.headline: SP names five UP candidates while Congress seat talks continue, drawing Congress objection
stories.dek: Congress MP Imran Masood questioned the Samajwadi Party's seriousness after the list, which includes two seats in Saharanpur, followed an offer of 26 seats to Congress.
stories.summary: The Samajwadi Party released its first list of five candidates for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh elections on Tuesday, hours after offering Congress 26 seats. Congress leader Imran Masood questioned the SP's seriousness; SP's Shivpal Yadav said the alliance would remain intact.
body: The Samajwadi Party on Tuesday evening named five candidates for next year's Uttar Pradesh assembly elections while seat-sharing talks with the Congress were still on, prompting Congress MP Imran Masood to question the SP's seriousness about the alliance.

The list names Umar Ali Khan (Behat), Ashu Malik (Saharanpur), Nahid Hasan (Kairana), Mehboob Ali (Amroha) and Jyoti Lodhi (Lalitpur). Hindustan Times reported that four are sitting MLAs and that Lodhi is a former party district president contesting a seat held by the BJP. NDTV reported that four of the five seats are in western Uttar Pradesh.

The announcement came hours after the SP made what Hindustan Times called an opening offer of 26 of the state's 403 seats to Congress at talks in Delhi. SP general secretary Ram Gopal Yadav said the offer includes two seats Congress won in 2022, four where it finished second and 20 where the SP believes Congress is weaker, according to News18.

Congress has reduced its demand from 181 seats. Sources told NDTV the party sought 131 at a first meeting on Monday and 110 on Tuesday; The Economic Times, citing Congress sources, reported that it submitted a list of 120 and would not accept fewer. The SP kept to 26, NDTV reported.

Masood, the Congress's Uttar Pradesh working president and the Saharanpur MP, was quoted by PTI as saying: "While you [Samajwadi Party] are holding talks on one side, you are making declarations on the other. This indicates that the matter is not being taken seriously." He said the party would decide whether to continue talks. News18 quoted him as saying: "Are we beggars?"

Behat and Saharanpur were reportedly among seats Congress sought, though neither side has confirmed the list. NDTV's sources said Congress was considering fielding its own candidate in Saharanpur. Congress has not officially responded to the list, NDTV reported.
SP leader Shivpal Yadav, quoted by PTI, said: "There is no rift in the alliance, the alliance will remain intact."

Akhilesh Yadav said in a post on X that the 26 seats were a start and asked Congress to identify other seats for joint assessment. Scroll quoted him as saying: "This is not about seats, but about victory."

BJP MLA Rajeshwar Singh said on X that the SP had named candidates without asking Congress, despite Akhilesh Yadav's call for "seat adjustment". He also said four of the five tickets went to one community and none to Dalits.
News18 reported that Rahul Gandhi is expected to begin Congress's Uttar Pradesh campaign from Saharanpur in December.
keyFacts: SP named five candidates on Tuesday: Behat, Saharanpur, Kairana, Amroha and Lalitpur.
SP offered Congress 26 of 403 seats; Congress sources say they seek about 110 to 120.
Congress initially sought 181 seats, Akhilesh Yadav said on November 15.
In 2024 Lok Sabha polls, SP gave Congress 17 of 80 seats; Congress won six.
stories.background: The SP and Congress contested the 2022 assembly elections separately. They revived their alliance for the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, in which the SP won 37 of 62 seats it contested. In 2022 the BJP won 255 seats, the SP 111 and Congress two.
stories.whyItMatters: The dispute over seat numbers and candidates will shape whether the two main Opposition parties fight the BJP together in Uttar Pradesh in 2027.

stories.headline: China launches Shenzhou-24 with Pakistan's first astronaut bound for Tiangong
stories.dek: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a 40-year-old pilot, will be the first foreign astronaut to board China's space station, joining Chinese crew Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi.
stories.summary: China launched Shenzhou-24 on Wednesday from the Jiuquan centre with two Chinese astronauts and Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali. He is the first foreign national to go to the Tiangong space station and is due to stay five to 10 days.
body: China launched its Shenzhou-24 spacecraft on Wednesday carrying two Chinese astronauts and Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreign national to travel to the Tiangong space station.

A Long March-2F rocket lifted off at 8:18 am local time (0018 GMT, 5:48 am IST) from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China, according to The Hindu and NDTV. NDTV reported that Chinese officials called the launch a "complete success" and that the spacecraft entered its planned orbit.

Zeeshan Ali, 40, is a Pakistan Air Force pilot. He will serve as a payload specialist and conduct experiments during a stay of five to 10 days, The Hindu reported. The crew is commanded by Tang Hongbo, with Wu Yi as flight engineer.

Zeeshan Ali trained for seven months in Beijing, according to The Hindu. The training included intensive Chinese-language classes, and he also learned Chinese songs, read Chinese poetry, practised calligraphy and played table tennis.
"I'm not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder," he told reporters on Tuesday.

NDTV reported that about 200 candidates applied to Pakistan's astronaut programme, and that two finalists, both from the military, were chosen: Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud. Training in China began in 2025, and Zeeshan Ali was confirmed as the flyer a day before launch, the outlet said.
The South China Morning Post reported that for about a week the station will host four astronauts from mainland China, one from Hong Kong and one from Pakistan.
The Hindu said China is promoting Tiangong as a hub for international cooperation, while the NASA-led International Space Station faces possible retirement by 2030.
keyFacts: Shenzhou-24 lifted off on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre.
Crew: Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40.
Zeeshan Ali is due to stay at Tiangong for 5 to 10 days.
He trained for seven months in Beijing before the flight.
stories.background: In 2023, Namira Salim became the first Pakistani to travel to space, aboard a Virgin Galactic suborbital tourism flight lasting a few minutes, NDTV reported. Zeeshan Ali's mission is to an orbiting station. NDTV also said China and Pakistan have broadened cooperation in satellite technology, communications, Earth observation and remote sensing over the past decade.
stories.whyItMatters: The flight opens China's Tiangong station to a foreign astronaut for the first time, as China promotes the station for international cooperation.

stories.headline: Trump says pardon for Nvidia's Jensen Huang is 'an option' but likely unneeded
stories.dek: Huang told staff he made 'terrible mistakes' and is in daily therapy, a day after the board reinstated him following Trump's intervention.
stories.summary: President Donald Trump told the New York Post a pardon for reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is 'always an option' but probably unnecessary. Huang apologised to staff, and Attorney General Todd Blanche declined to say whether Nvidia is under investigation.
body: US President Donald Trump said in a New York Post interview on Tuesday that a pardon for Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang is "always an option", though he does not expect to need one, as Huang prepares to face Congress.

"It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump said. He added that Huang does not need to "take the Fifth", a reference to the constitutional right against self-incrimination, and that he wanted him to "just tell the truth". Trump said he had always found Huang "100 per cent aboveboard". Trump also said he had considered a US government stake in Nvidia, adding: "It's probably not too late."

Asked about Huang's extramarital affairs, Trump said he "really didn't get into that" and had focused on "the business of chips". The Daily Wire noted that public reporting has not established that Huang himself is under criminal investigation or committed a crime.

Nvidia's board reinstated Huang on Monday, less than two weeks after he was forced out over revelations of an affair with a subordinate and another with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy. Trump said he spoke to the directors and persuaded them. The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident there was no national security risk.

At an all-hands meeting at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Tuesday, Huang apologised to staff, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke to Bloomberg. BBC News reported he said he made "terrible mistakes" and is in therapy for 90 minutes a day. Huang acknowledged breaching the company's code of conduct and said he was not reinstated because he is above the law, the people said.

Shortly before, Attorney General Todd Blanche called Nvidia a "good corporate citizen" but declined to say whether the Justice Department is examining the events behind Huang's exit. Asked whether the department or FBI had investigated Huang, he said: "I don't know what you're talking about." Commerce and justice departments said last week they began investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer, in 2024 over potential export control violations. Blanche said the department runs "hundreds, if not more" export investigations at once.

Lawmakers in both parties have objected. Republican Senator Dave McCormick warned of a "slippery slope" in corporate governance. Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress should investigate stock positions taken before the announcement.

Nvidia shares rose about 31% on Monday and fell nearly 6% on Tuesday. Huang is due to give a closed-door interview to three House committees on December 1 and testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3, according to the Daily Wire.
keyFacts: Trump told the New York Post a pardon is 'always an option' but probably unnecessary.
Nvidia's board reinstated Huang on Monday, less than two weeks after he was forced out.
Nvidia shares rose about 31% on Monday and closed down nearly 6% on Tuesday.
Huang is due before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3.
stories.background: Huang resigned as CEO after revelations of affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert restricted chips to China. US commerce officials said they were preparing to blacklist Megaspeed.
stories.whyItMatters: Congress will question Huang and Nvidia over export controls on advanced chips and national security, while the president's role in a private company's board decision has drawn bipartisan objections.

perspectives.summary: Trump says he trusts Huang, wants him to tell the truth and sees no national security risk. Blanche said Nvidia is a good corporate citizen and warned against treating unverified reports as fact.

perspectives.summary: Republicans and Democrats question Trump's role in the reinstatement and want answers on national security, unaccounted-for chips and pre-announcement stock trades.

stories.headline: CIA and intelligence director's office hit by breach of unclassified data
stories.dek: The affected network was used to analyse open-source intelligence, and sources say no classified systems were touched and the issue has been resolved.
stories.summary: The CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence discovered hackers had accessed an unclassified open-source analysis network, the New York Times reported on Tuesday. It is the latest in a run of cyber incidents at US agencies.
body: The CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) recently discovered that hackers had accessed an unclassified network used to analyse open-source intelligence, the New York Times reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.

A person familiar with the incident told The Associated Press that the breach involved no classified information and had been resolved. An ODNI official said there had been "no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems." The CIA declined to comment, according to the Times.

Open-source intelligence draws on publicly available material such as social media posts, satellite imagery and commercially available data. Investigators have not said publicly what information was accessed, who was responsible or how the intruders got in.

Mint, citing the Times, reported that the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency was also affected. It said the hackers used an AI tool called Artex, released in July by a Chinese engineer and intended for cyber defence. Cybersecurity researchers have since linked it to attacks on businesses in countries including Japan and South Korea, according to that report.

Mint reported that initial indications, including the use of the tool, point to possible Chinese involvement, citing Western officials. No attribution has been established. Fox News, citing sources, said it was unclear who was behind the breach or whether the intrusions were connected.

Fox News reported that the CIA, ODNI and FBI were breached on the same day last week. The FBI incident involved the National Crime Information Center, a database local, state and federal law enforcement agencies use to share information on criminal suspects, missing persons and stolen property. The FBI is continuing its investigation.
President Donald Trump acknowledged the FBI breach in a phone interview with Fox News on Saturday. "I will say that it's not good — I don't like that," he said.

The Department of Agriculture also discovered a cybersecurity incident last week that took some internal applications offline. Separately, the National Security Agency's classified network, NSANet, suffered an outage. The agency described it as scheduled routine maintenance and has not called it a cyberattack. Fox News reported that the outage stemmed from an internal technology upgrade. Two Pentagon officials told Fox News the Department of War was not breached.

Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, whom Trump recently named acting national cyber director, addressed the incidents on television on Sunday. "Cyberprobing, cyberincidents, they have been part of the American economy, part of the American life for a long time," he said on ABC's "This Week" about the FBI breach.
keyFacts: The CIA and ODNI found hackers had accessed an unclassified open-source intelligence analysis network, the New York Times reported on Tuesday.
Sources say no classified systems were affected and the issue has been resolved.
Mint, citing the Times, said the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency was also affected and that initial indications point to China.
The FBI's National Crime Information Center was breached in a separate incident last week.
Jay Clayton is both director of national intelligence and acting national cyber director.
stories.background: Open-source intelligence analysis combines public information with other sources to support assessments. Mint reported that some commercially sold data can reveal sensitive details when analysed alongside other datasets. Federal agencies have faced several incidents in recent weeks, including the FBI breach, an Agriculture Department incident and an NSA network outage that the agency has not attributed to hacking.
stories.whyItMatters: The incidents involve systems at several federal agencies, including a database that police across the US use to share information on suspects and missing persons.

stories.headline: Madurai police book about 300 BJP, Hindu group members over Thiruparankundram protests
stories.dek: The Karthigai Deepam was lit at the Uchi Pillayar mandapam, not the stone pillar the Supreme Court had named in an interim order; the temple cites Agama rules.
stories.summary: Madurai Police registered cases against about 300 BJP and Hindu organisation members who protested at Thiruparankundram on Tuesday. The lamp was lit at the traditional Uchi Pillayar spot, not the Deepathoon pillar named in a Supreme Court interim order.
body: Madurai Police have registered cases against about 300 members of the BJP and Hindu organisations for protesting at Thiruparankundram on Tuesday, after the Karthigai Deepam was lit at the Uchi Pillayar temple and not at the Deepathoon stone pillar, news agency ANI reported, citing police, on Wednesday.

Police said the cases were filed under six sections, including unlawful assembly without permission, causing a breach of public peace, making controversial remarks and obstructing government servants in their duty.

On November 20, a Supreme Court Bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul Pancholi ordered the lamp to be lit at the pillar on the day of the festival, calling it a "temporary, one-time arrangement". The order came on the Tamil Nadu government's plea to stay a January 6 judgment. The court directed that the lamp be lit at 6pm.

The Maha Deepam was lit at about 6pm at the Uchipillayar Deepa Mandapam, a small team of priests from the Subramaniya Swamy temple performing the ceremony. The Hindu reported that around 6,000 police personnel were deployed across Madurai and the hillock under a prohibitory order. No lamp was lit at the pillar.

The temple's Executive Officer G. Selvi and Board of Trustees chairman V. Shanmugasundaram said in a joint press release that the temple followed age-old custom and Agama rules. NDTV reported the board said the lamp is lit only at the mandapam because it sits directly above the presiding deity, and that these customs should be placed before the Supreme Court.

Petitioner and Hindu Munnani advocate Niranjan S Kumar said the order was violated. "I would say it was not only violated, but it is a deliberate, calculated and willful disobedience of the order of the Supreme Court," he said, adding that petitioners would approach the court for contempt. He noted the court had told the Madurai District Collector to file a status report within three days of the festival.

Tamil Nadu BJP leader Tamilisai Soundararajan said she "strongly condemn[ed] the TVK government for violating the Supreme Court's interim order". She alleged BJP leaders and workers were kept away from the temple while leaders of some other parties were allowed in. BJP state president Nainar Nagenthran was arrested in Tirunelveli district on his way to Thiruparankundram, The Hindu reported.

The Hindu reported that police detained protesters outside the temple, saying some resisted and tried to damage public property. Protests were also reported in Ramanathapuram, Pollachi and Chennai, where police detained or removed demonstrators who blocked roads.

The Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court on Tuesday issued an order restraining members of the public from calling for violation of the Supreme Court order. It recorded the Collector's assurance that steps were being taken to comply.
keyFacts: About 300 BJP and Hindu organisation members booked under six sections by Madurai Police.
Supreme Court ordered the lamp lit at the Deepathoon pillar on November 20, as a one-time arrangement.
Lamp was lit at the Uchipillayar Deepa Mandapam around 6pm on Tuesday, November 24.
Madurai Collector must file a status report within three days of the festival.
Around 6,000 police personnel were deployed in Madurai and on the hillock.
stories.background: The Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy Temple, one of the six abodes of Lord Murugan, stands at the foot of Thiruparankundram hill. The summit has the Sikandar Badusha Dargah, and the Deepathoon stone pillar is about 50 metres from it. The dispute is over whether the Karthigai Deepam should also be lit at the pillar. The Hindu cited a state government report saying the structure is a survey pillar.
stories.whyItMatters: Petitioners say they will seek contempt proceedings, so the Collector's status report to the Supreme Court may shape the next stage of the case.

perspectives.label: BJP and Hindu organisations
perspectives.summary: They say the state deliberately defied the Supreme Court's interim order by not lighting the lamp at the pillar, and that BJP workers were arrested while others were let near the temple.

perspectives.label: Temple administration
perspectives.summary: The temple says it lit the lamp at the traditional mandapam under age-old custom and Agama rules, and that these practices should be put before the Supreme Court.

perspectives.label: Police and state authorities
perspectives.summary: Police say the protesters assembled without permission, and that some resisted detention and tried to damage property. The Collector told the High Court that steps were being taken to comply with the Supreme Court.

stories.headline: Akali Dal and BJP announce alliance for 2027 Punjab Assembly elections
stories.dek: Home Minister Amit Shah said the Akalis would be the senior partner and would claim the chief minister's post if the NDA wins; Congress attacked the tie-up over the farm laws.
stories.summary: The Shiromani Akali Dal and the BJP announced on Tuesday that they will fight the Punjab Assembly elections together, six years after the Akalis left the NDA over the farm laws. Congress said the pact ignores farmers' sacrifices.
body: The Shiromani Akali Dal and the Bharatiya Janata Party announced in New Delhi on Tuesday that they will contest the 2027 Punjab Assembly elections together, six years after the Akalis walked out of the National Democratic Alliance over the farm laws.

Union Home Minister Amit Shah made the announcement alongside SAD president Sukhbir Singh Badal and BJP president Nitin Nabin. The timing coincided with Guru Nanak's birth anniversary. The Times of India reported that Shah described the SAD as the "big brother" in the arrangement and the claimant to the chief minister's post if the NDA wins. No chief ministerial face was formally named, though the newspaper described Badal as the obvious choice.

Shah said: "The alliance between BJP and SAD is not merely political; it is an emotional bond rooted in mutual trust and Punjab's history. NDA is now complete with Akali Dal's return." Badal said "a tidal wave has started today" and claimed the alliance would win 100 seats in the 117-member Assembly.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi called it a "natural alliance". He is due to attend a rally in Moga on December 8 marking the birth anniversary of Parkash Singh Badal. The Times of India said a meeting between Modi and Sukhbir Badal at the Parliament complex on August 7 was the first clear sign of the tie-up. It also reported that the BJP is expected to contest more than the 23 seats it used to under the earlier alliance.

The Punjab Congress responded on Wednesday. In a post on X, it said Badal had been "exposed for crawling back to the BJP" after calling it "anti-farmer" and "anti-Punjab", and called the alliance one forged "purely out of greed for power". It added: "Punjabis will not forget the sacrifices made at the Delhi border during the farm agitation."

Sachin Pilot, the Congress general secretary in charge of Punjab, called it "a compromised alliance, a desperate alliance". He asked whether the Centre had given any guarantee on MSP or apologised for the farm laws. Leader of Opposition Partap Singh Bajwa called it a "desperate marriage of political convenience between two rejected parties", and state president Pargat Singh called the deal a "betrayal of Punjab".

BJP MP Harbhajan Singh told CNN-News18 that the alliance would help because "when the government at the Centre and the state is the same, development can happen much faster". He listed drugs, sports, infrastructure and jobs for youth as priorities.
The Hindu reported that, with the old partners reunited, Punjab appears headed for a four-cornered contest. The election is due in early 2027.

The Akalis left the NDA in 2020 over the farm laws.

stories.background: The SAD and BJP governed Punjab together for a decade until their defeat by Congress in 2017. The Akalis withdrew their minister from the Union Cabinet and left the NDA in 2020 after the Centre introduced the farm laws, which were later repealed. The AAP won the state in 2022.
stories.whyItMatters: The pact reshapes the contest in Punjab, where the AAP and Congress had been seen as the main contenders, and returns the farm-law agitation to the centre of campaign debate.

stories.headline: US jury convicts Huawei on 10 of 12 counts, acquits it of racketeering
stories.dek: Jurors in Brooklyn found the company guilty of trade-secret theft, bank fraud and sanctions violations; Huawei says the remaining charges lack legal or factual merit and its lawyer expects an appeal.
stories.summary: A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Huawei and three subsidiaries on 10 of 12 counts on Tuesday, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud. It acquitted the company of racketeering conspiracy; sentencing is set for September 14, 2027.
body: A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Chinese telecommunications company Huawei and three of its subsidiaries on 10 of 12 criminal counts on Tuesday, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud and violations of US sanctions.

Jurors acquitted the company of racketeering conspiracy, which required them to find that Huawei operated as a criminal enterprise, and of conspiracy to obstruct justice. The other convictions included wire fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement: "For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft." The Justice Department said the company misrepresented its Iran operations to banks to obtain billions of US dollars and access to US-dollar clearing services.

Prosecutors said Huawei ran its Iran business through Skycom, a subsidiary it falsely described as an independent partner. The Justice Department also said Huawei supplied surveillance cameras that Iranian authorities used to monitor protests.

On trade secrets, prosecutors named Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu as victim companies. They said Huawei copied source code used in Cisco routers, and that employees sent photographs and technical details of T-Mobile's touchscreen-testing robot to China. One employee removed a component from T-Mobile's laboratory in a backpack, according to the Justice Department. DW also reported that an employee photographed circuit boards at a Chicago trade fair.

Huawei said the acquittal on racketeering "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis". It added: "We believe the government's remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit." The company said the five trade-secret disputes cited by prosecutors were civil matters resolved over the past two decades, and that no court found it liable for wilful misappropriation.
Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig told the BBC the racketeering count was "a significant overreach" and that Huawei had hoped for acquittals "across the board". He said: "We fully expect to appeal."
Sentencing is scheduled for September 14, 2027. The company could face criminal fines, forfeiture and restitution, which Daily Wire and DW reported could run to billions of dollars.
keyFacts: The jury convicted Huawei and three subsidiaries on 10 of 12 counts in a Brooklyn federal court.

stories.background: US prosecutors first disclosed criminal charges against Huawei in January 2019, a month after chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou was arrested in Canada. Meng returned to China in September 2021 under a deferred prosecution agreement. No individuals were defendants at this trial. Sources gave the trial's length as two months (BBC) and three months (Justice Department, CNBC, The Hindu).
stories.whyItMatters: The convictions expose Huawei to fines, forfeiture and restitution at sentencing. The company says it will pursue legal action and an appeal while maintaining uninterrupted business operations.

stories.headline: Rahul Gandhi says Rajiv Gandhi's security was withdrawn on purpose so he would be killed
stories.dek: The Leader of the Opposition made the claim in a video conversation with Sonia Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra about her memoir, 'Belonging: A Journey of Love'.
stories.summary: Rahul Gandhi said in a video released on Tuesday that his father Rajiv Gandhi's security was removed deliberately so that he would be killed. Reports note the SPG Act of 1988 covered only serving Prime Ministers.
body: Lok Sabha Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi said on Tuesday that the security cover of his father, former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi, was withdrawn deliberately so that he would be assassinated.
He made the remark in a video conversation with his mother, Sonia Gandhi, and sister, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, about her memoir, 'Belonging: A Journey of Love'. The video was released on November 24.

"My position on it is very clear: Papa's security was removed so that he got killed. Papa's security removal was not just an accident, it was done on purpose. So that he got killed and the atmosphere was created for him to get killed," Gandhi said.

According to The Times of India, he added that he had told his parents about it and argued with his father. The newspaper said the remark followed Sonia Gandhi's account of lax security during Rajiv Gandhi's visit to Bihar as Opposition leader, where he faced stone pelting. Rahul Gandhi had accompanied him.
In a post on X, Rahul Gandhi wrote: "There was an intention behind withdrawing Papa's security."

The Times of India noted that the Special Protection Group Act, passed in 1988 under Rajiv Gandhi's government, limited SPG cover to the Prime Minister and not former Prime Ministers. Rajiv Gandhi therefore lost it after the 1989 election defeat, the paper said.

The Hindu reported that the V.P. Singh government withdrew his SPG cover in February 1990, and that responsibility for his security outside Delhi passed to state governments. He was killed by a Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam suicide bomber at Sriperumbudur, Tamil Nadu, on May 21, 1991, when the state was under President's Rule. The Times of India said the Chandra Shekhar government was in office at the time.

After the assassination, the P.V. Narasimha Rao government amended the Act to cover former Prime Ministers and their immediate families for five years, the paper said. A 1994 amendment extended this to 10 years.
Rahul Gandhi also said his mother had not written about how she was treated by some people in politics. He said she was "humiliated, abused" and that he might speak about it someday.

The family also discussed earlier years, including the period after the Emergency. Priyanka Gandhi Vadra recalled slapping a classmate who taunted her over the arrest of her uncle, Sanjay Gandhi. HarperCollins India CEO Ananth Padmanabhan said the memoir has sold over two lakh copies in under a week.

stories.headline: China investigates Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, a Politburo member
stories.dek: Chen, 62, is the fourth of the 24 Politburo members appointed in 2022 to come under investigation, leaving the body with 21 active members, Bloomberg reported.
stories.summary: China's anti-corruption body is investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected serious violations of discipline and law, Xinhua reported on Tuesday. Chen, long seen as a possible future national leader, is the fourth 2022 Politburo member to be probed.
body: China's top anti-corruption body has opened an investigation into Chen Jining, the Communist Party chief of Shanghai and a member of the Politburo, the state news agency Xinhua reported on Tuesday.

Xinhua said Chen, 62, is suspected of "serious violations of discipline and the law". It gave no details of the alleged wrongdoing. The phrase is commonly used in China to refer to corruption, according to The Guardian and The New York Times.

Shanghai's party standing committee said it firmly supports the decision. Its statement said the probe showed Beijing's determination to press on with its anti-corruption campaign, Bloomberg reported. The city's official newspaper said on Wednesday that Shanghai's senior leaders pledged loyalty to Beijing and said they understood the need to "see things through to the end".

Chen is the fourth of the 24 Politburo members appointed in 2022 to be investigated, after military leaders He Weidong and Zhang Youxia and former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui. Bloomberg reported that he has not been removed from the Politburo, which now has 21 active members, the fewest since 1999.

Chen had been widely viewed as a contender for higher office, and analysts said the announcement came as a surprise. Taisu Zhang, a Yale Law School professor, wrote on X that Chen had been seen as "a near-lock for the politburo Standing Committee". Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt of the University of Zurich told The Guardian the case "sends a signal that there's no letting up in the anti-corruption drive".

Neil Thomas, a senior analyst at Bloomberg Economics, said the case showed the fragility of business strategies built around access to individual leaders. Chen had hosted visitors including Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Apple's Tim Cook and Citigroup's Jane Fraser, and had promoted artificial intelligence, semiconductors and biomedicine in the city. He made a public appearance on November 19, visiting COSCO Shipping's headquarters.
On Weibo, the hashtag "Chen Jining under investigation" had drawn about 240m views by Wednesday morning, The Guardian reported.
The party is preparing for a congress in the second half of next year, when Xi Jinping is expected to secure another five years in power and name a new leadership team.
keyFacts: Xinhua announced the investigation into Chen Jining on Tuesday, November 24.
Chen is 62 and has been Shanghai party secretary and a Politburo member since 2022.
He is the fourth 2022 Politburo member probed, after He Weidong, Zhang Youxia and Ma Xingrui.
The Politburo now has 21 active members, the fewest since 1999, Bloomberg reported.
Chen appeared in public on November 19 at COSCO Shipping's headquarters.
stories.background:
Chen studied environmental engineering at Tsinghua University and earned a doctorate from Imperial College London. He became Tsinghua's president in 2012, led the environmental protection ministry from 2015 to 2017, and later served as Beijing mayor, overseeing the 2022 Winter Olympics.

Shanghai's party chief post has often led to higher office. Xi Jinping led the city in 2007 and months later joined the Politburo Standing Committee. Chen is the first Shanghai party chief to be investigated in two decades, Bloomberg reported.
stories.whyItMatters: The case removes a senior figure once seen as a candidate for national leadership before the party congress next year. Bloomberg Economics said businesses and investors that relied on access to individual leaders face exposure.

stories.headline: Solomon Islands signs treaty naming Australia primary security partner
stories.dek: The pact bars foreign military bases on Solomon Islands soil, while Prime Minister Matthew Wale declines to confirm reports that the 2022 China agreement will not be renewed.
stories.summary: Australia and Solomon Islands signed a treaty in Canberra on Wednesday making Australia the country's primary security partner and barring foreign military bases. Honiara has not confirmed reports that it told Beijing its 2022 security pact will lapse.
body: Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale signed a treaty in Canberra on Wednesday that makes Australia the Pacific nation's "primary security partner" and states there will be no foreign military or security base on its territory.

Wale would not confirm or deny reports that his government had told Beijing it would not renew the 2022 security pact with China, which expires in early 2027. He cited a non-disclosure clause. "We have ongoing discussions with China," he said.

A diplomatic official with knowledge of the matter, speaking anonymously to The New York Times, said Honiara notified Beijing last month that the agreement would not be renewed. Australian media reported on Tuesday that Honiara had given that notice.

The treaty commits Solomon Islands to keep sensitive infrastructure "free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access". CNA reported that this covers airports, ports, energy and telecommunications, and will not apply retrospectively. Honiara must also consult Australia before security or critical infrastructure deals with countries outside the Pacific Islands Forum, of which China is not a member.

Australia will provide AU$740 million over 10 years, made up of AU$670 million in grants and AU$70 million in concessional loans, according to CNA and The Guardian. The money is to support education, health, policing, resources and climate resilience, and is expected to flow from January. The package also covers improved visa arrangements, an expanded labour mobility scheme and funding for a football club.
The Guardian reported that about 14 Chinese police officers posted under the existing deal are expected to leave by the middle of 2027.

"Those days are done. Gone," Wale said of the country's past as "a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region". Albanese said Australia would act in a way that "completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions".

China's foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, did not say on Tuesday whether the pact had been ended. He said cooperation between China and Pacific island countries involves "no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation".

Opposition leader Manasseh Sogavare, who signed the China pact as prime minister, criticised the "fast-tracking" of the Australian treaty while the status of the China arrangement remained "unclear", CNA reported.
Wale said his entire cabinet approved the treaty. Solomon Islands officials told AFP that parliament will return in January to consider reforms, including free education.
keyFacts: The treaty was signed in Canberra on Wednesday, November 25, 2026.
Australia will provide AU$740 million over 10 years: AU$670 million in grants, AU$70 million in loans.
The China pact, signed in 2022, expires in early 2027 and has not been confirmed as ended.

Solomon Islands parliament is due to return in January.
stories.background: Solomon Islands signed a security pact with China in 2022 under then prime minister Manasseh Sogavare. The agreement raised fears in Australia and the US that Chinese naval ships or troops could gain a presence in the Pacific. Australia has since signed security alliances or wide-ranging treaties with five other Pacific island countries, according to CNA. Wale became prime minister in May.
stories.whyItMatters: The treaty sets Australia's security role in Solomon Islands and ties new funding to education, health and policing. A third of Solomon Islands children do not start school, according to reports.

stories.headline: AI stocks fall again in US and Asia; Anthropic closes below $83 IPO price
stories.dek: SoftBank lost 15% and Japan's chip stocks dropped sharply on Wednesday after Nvidia gave back part of its 30% gain from Jensen Huang's return as CEO.
stories.summary: Nvidia fell almost 6% on Tuesday, a day after surging more than 30%, and Anthropic closed at $81.90, below its $83 IPO price. Asian technology stocks tumbled on Wednesday, with SoftBank down 15%.
body: Technology shares fell on Wall Street on Tuesday and Asian tech stocks dropped sharply on Wednesday, reversing the rally that followed Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive and pushing newly listed Anthropic below its IPO price.

The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.48% and the S&P 500 lost 0.5%, according to The Guardian. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended slightly higher; NDTV reported a gain of more than 400 points. Nvidia shares lost almost 6%, after rising more than 30% on Monday and adding more than $900bn to its market value, The Guardian reported.

Anthropic shares closed down 6.5% at $81.90, below the $83 price at which it sold stock last week, CNBC and The Guardian reported. The stock opened at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on November 19 after the company raised $81.3 billion, which CNBC described as the largest offering of all time. The Wall Street Journal reported that the shares have now fallen for three straight sessions.
NDTV reported that the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 7.6%, with Micron down more than 10% and Advanced Micro Devices down roughly 9%.

In Asia on Wednesday, CNBC reported that SoftBank Group lost 15%. Advantest fell 13%, Tokyo Electron 12.82%, Lasertec 11.23%, Disco 9.41% and Renesas Electronics 9%. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix each fell more than 8%. In Taiwan, TSMC dropped 7% and Hon Hai Precision Industry 8.6%.
Some Hong Kong-listed Chinese technology stocks rose. Xiaomi gained 4.6% and Kuaishou 2.8%, while Alibaba added 0.7%, CNBC said.

Analysts tied the moves to doubts about AI spending. Rolf Bulk of The Futurum Group said: "There are still concerns on the sustainability of AI demand, ability of the sector to finance the build-out, and questions around power supply." He said Huang's return did little to change the outlook.

Kathleen Brooks of XTB said Nvidia's fall was "to be expected after such a large rally in the previous session". The Guardian reported that analysts saw Huang's return as ending neither the investigations into Nvidia nor the uncertainty around AI stocks. Nvidia remains under scrutiny from investigators including the FBI and Capitol Hill over allegations that it helped Chinese firms gain access to its top chips.

Analysts remain largely positive on Anthropic. Canaccord Genuity began coverage with a buy rating and a $135 price target, Oppenheimer set $150, and Wedbush set $120, CNBC reported. Canaccord said the risks are "unusually large", particularly around infrastructure commitments.

The Nasdaq fell 1.48% and the S&P 500 lost 0.5% on Tuesday.
SoftBank Group fell 15% in Asian trading on Wednesday.
Advantest dropped 13% and Tokyo Electron 12.82% in Japan.
stories.background: Huang resigned as Nvidia chief executive less than two weeks ago, according to The Guardian, and was reinstated on Monday. AI stocks had already sold off through November on worries about profitability and the scale of spending on the sector.
stories.whyItMatters: Investors in AI-linked chipmakers, equipment suppliers and Anthropic's new shareholders face continued price swings as doubts persist over whether heavy AI spending can be sustained.

stories.headline: Sensex jumps over 1,300 points in early trade on foreign inflows, softer crude
stories.dek: The rupee gained 23 paise to 92.62 against the dollar as Indian shares rose while South Korean, Japanese and Chinese markets fell.
stories.summary: The Sensex and Nifty rose sharply in early trade on Wednesday, the first session after a holiday, helped by foreign fund buying and lower crude prices. The rupee gained 23 paise to 92.62 against the US dollar.
body: The 30-share BSE Sensex jumped 1,382.16 points to 83,818.15 in early trade on Wednesday, while the 50-share NSE Nifty rose 407.60 points to 25,758.45, according to The Hindu. Buying in large bank stocks, foreign fund inflows and lower crude oil prices supported the rally.

Business Standard reported a slightly higher peak, with the Sensex up 1,466.70 points, or 1.78%, at 83,902.69 and the Nifty up 411.95 points at 25,761.60. Mint said the Sensex touched an intraday high of 83,869.60 and the Nifty reached 25,992.60. Figures differ by the time each outlet recorded them.

Among Sensex stocks, HDFC Bank rose 3.54%, Infosys 3.43%, ICICI Bank 3.19%, Bajaj Finance 2.65%, Axis Bank 2.13% and Bajaj Finserv 2.09%. Tata Steel, Mahindra & Mahindra, Titan and Power Grid traded lower. Mint reported that media and metal shares were the weakest sectors.

Markets were shut on Tuesday for Guru Nanak Jayanti. On Monday, both indices fell about 1.8% after profit booking that followed a four-week winning streak, Mint reported. The Sensex and Nifty are still up 10.7% and 10% respectively in November.

Foreign institutional investors bought equities worth ₹5,672.99 crore on Monday, according to exchange data. V K Vijayakumar, chief investment strategist at Geojit Investments, said foreign investment into India this month stood at a record $13.2 billion. Mint cited a figure of $14.28 billion from a separate source.
Brent crude traded 1.42% lower at $90.12 per barrel, per The Hindu. Mint said oil has fallen around 23% so far in November.

The rupee opened at 92.65 and rose to 92.62 against the dollar, up 23 paise from its previous close, Business Standard reported. Forex traders said a strong dollar capped gains. Mint reported a smaller rise of 10 paise to 92.75 at an earlier point in trade. The rupee had closed at 92.85 on Monday.

Asian markets were weaker. South Korea's Kospi fell 5.30% and Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 2.74%, according to The Hindu, while Shanghai's SSE Composite declined 1%. Vijayakumar attributed the global volatility mainly to swings in AI-related trade.
Shrikant Chouhan of Kotak Neo said the market could consolidate in a 25,000–26,000 range for the Nifty, with 25,600 on the Nifty and 83,300 on the Sensex as the immediate resistance zone.

stories.headline: Passport office bars CJP's Saurav Das from foreign travel pending reply on birth details
stories.dek: The Chennai Regional Passport Office gave Das until November 30 to explain alleged mismatches in his documents; he says the notice is meant to harass him.
stories.summary: The Regional Passport Office in Chennai has served CJP's Saurav Das a show-cause notice over alleged discrepancies in his birth details and told him not to use his passport. Das, stopped at Delhi airport before a UK flight, says the Centre is blocking his trip.
body: The Regional Passport Office (RPO) in Chennai has served Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leader Saurav Das a show-cause notice over alleged discrepancies in his birth details and told him not to use his passport, after he was stopped at Delhi's IGI airport before a flight to the UK.

According to The Times of India, the notice was emailed on Monday evening. It asks Das to respond within seven days to alleged "material suppression of facts" about his place of birth, with supporting documents. Failure to give a satisfactory explanation could lead to his passport being impounded under Section 10(b) of the Passports Act, 1967.

Government sources told the paper that mismatches in his date of birth, place of birth and father's name across Aadhaar, passport and school or birth certificates were flagged in inputs over recent months. The documents were issued in Delhi and Puducherry. The passport was issued on August 21, 2019. Officials said Das has until November 30 to reply and can travel again on the same passport once the RPO clears him in the re-verification.

Das said at a news conference on Tuesday that the notice reached him about five hours before his 1am flight and that he did not see it until he was at the immigration counter. He said it did not set out the grounds for the alleged inputs. He asked why the issue had not been raised earlier, given that his passport was issued after police verification and he had travelled abroad since.

"The notice was sent just five hours before my flight, and its sole purpose was to harass me and send a message to other young people: look, this could happen to you too," Das told reporters, according to Hindustan Times.

An unnamed officer told The Times of India that Das knew the pending notice would be flagged in immigration systems and went to the airport "possibly so he could play the victim". Das has not accepted that account.

Das said he was to speak at the Oxford Union on December 1 and at other UK institutions, some of them at the invitation of student groups. The LSESU Amnesty International Society said its event with him was postponed indefinitely and called the obstruction "arbitrary". Oxford Union did not respond to the Times of India.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke asked at a news conference in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, "Is Saurav a criminal? Has he looted a bank?" Delhi BJP spokesperson Praveen Shankar Kapoor said Das "wanted to slip out to defame India from abroad" and was going to a private body "to spew anti-India venom". The central government had not commented on the allegations, Hindustan Times reported.
Separately, the Madras High Court issued notice on October 30 to the Regional Passport Officer, Chennai, on a PIL alleging Das is not an Indian citizen and seeking cancellation of his passport.

stories.headline: Bengal minister Arjun Singh says India will 'take Bangladesh by December 16'
stories.dek: The remark on alleged killings of Hindus came as Dhaka said Sheikh Hasina would be arrested in handcuffs if she returned on that date.
stories.summary: West Bengal minister Arjun Singh told reporters in Bhatpara that India would 'take Bangladesh by December 16' and avenge killings of Hindus there. Dhaka has said Sheikh Hasina, who plans to return on that date, would be arrested.
body: West Bengal minister Arjun Singh said on Tuesday that India would "take Bangladesh by December 16" and that killings of Hindus in Bangladesh would be avenged, according to The Times of India and Hindustan Times.

Speaking to reporters in Bhatpara, Singh said: "We will take Bangladesh by December 16th. Enough is enough; there are no more excuses regarding Bangladesh. We will certainly take revenge for the way Hindus have been killed in Bangladesh; there is no doubt about that." The sources do not say what he meant by "take", and they carry no response from the Indian or Bangladeshi governments to his remarks.

The date matches the one set by former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina for her proposed return. Her spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, told Reuters she intends to travel from Delhi to Dhaka on December 16 on Biman Bangladesh Airlines. December 16 is Bangladesh's Victory Day.

In an official communication, Ali said Hasina had asked Dhaka to arrange her air transport. "Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5, 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he said, according to Reuters.

Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, Humayun Kobir, rejected the plan after briefing foreign diplomats in Dhaka. "Desire and reality are two different things," he said. He added that she "can only be brought back in handcuffs and under strict surveillance" and that a "terrorist" would not be allowed to return except through extradition.

International Crimes Tribunal chief prosecutor Md Aminul Islam reportedly described her request for a state aircraft as "nothing but madness". A Bangladeshi minister told Reuters on Sunday that she would face immediate arrest and imprisonment, and that no formal talks had been held with India on a plane.

Hasina was prime minister from 2009 until 2024. She fled to India on August 5, 2024, after a student-led agitation over public sector job quotas grew into a nationwide uprising. The International Crimes Tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over the crackdown on protesters. She has denied the allegations.

Earlier this month she applied for a new passport and national identity card through her lawyers in the United Kingdom. Dhaka has repeatedly sought her extradition, and New Delhi has said the request is under examination.
keyFacts: Arjun Singh made the remarks to reporters in Bhatpara on Tuesday.
Hasina's spokesperson says she plans to fly from Delhi to Dhaka on December 16.
Dhaka's Humayun Kobir said she could return only 'in handcuffs'.
Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia by Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal; she denies the charges.
India says Dhaka's extradition request is under examination.
stories.background: Hasina fled to India on August 5, 2024, after a student-led uprising against her Awami League government. Bangladesh's tribunal later sentenced her to death in absentia, and Dhaka has asked India repeatedly to extradite her.
stories.whyItMatters: The remark adds a political voice from an Indian state government to a dispute between New Delhi and Dhaka over Hasina's stay in India and her announced return date.

stories.headline: Kuki and Naga leaders agree to start peace process in Manipur, urge Christmas truce
stories.dek: The agreement followed a three-day summit in Kolkata; the leaders also plan another round of dialogue before Christmas, with all stakeholders invited.
stories.summary: Kuki and Naga Christian and civil society leaders said on Tuesday they had agreed to begin a process to address the causes of conflict between the two communities in Manipur. The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, which organised the talks, asked both communities to observe a Christmas truce.
body: Kuki and Naga leaders representing Christian and civil society groups said on Tuesday they had agreed to begin a "forward-looking" process to identify and address the problems fuelling the conflict between the two ethnic communities in Manipur.
The agreement was reached at the Kuki-Naga Prayer and Peace Summit, held in Kolkata from Sunday to Tuesday. The Forum for Naga Reconciliation organised the meeting.

In a statement, the forum said leaders from both communities "engaged in an honest, open-spirited and respectful dialogue" and "recognised and acknowledged how deeply they have hurt one another". It said the groups also saw a need to explore ways to "break the chain of fear, hate and violence".

The forum said it was asking the two communities to "work towards a Christmas truce". It described the truce as a confidence-building measure that should bring immediate relief to affected families and "end the cycle of violence and prevent further escalation and the loss of human lives". It would also allow community leaders to begin "real dialogue around the underlying core issues of the conflict", the forum said.

The Kuki side was represented by Kuki Christian Churches Manipur, Kuki Baptist Churches Manipur, Kuki Inpi Manipur, Kuki Christian Leader's Forum, Kuki Baptist Association Nagaland and Kuki Christian Church Nagaland. The Naga side was represented by Naga Christian Forum Manipur, Naga Peoples' Initiative for Peace Manipur, Fellowship of Naga Baptist Association and the United Naga Council.

The statement said the leaders accepted that "the road to peace is not a quick-fix, but one that requires political and moral courage and willingness to be part of a sustained and broader dialogue to peace". To consolidate the process, they agreed to hold another round of dialogue before Christmas, to which all stakeholders would be invited.

The summit also appealed for an end to what the forum called the "violence of words" on social media. "The lies, rumours, hatred and propaganda are instilling more animosity and polarisation. This must end immediately," the forum said.
Scroll reported that 72 people have died in clashes between the two communities in Manipur since February.
keyFacts: The Kuki-Naga Prayer and Peace Summit was held in Kolkata from Sunday to Tuesday.
The Forum for Naga Reconciliation organised the summit and issued the statement.
Leaders agreed to another round of dialogue before Christmas, with all stakeholders invited.
Scroll reports 72 deaths in Kuki-Naga clashes in Manipur since February.
stories.background: Scroll reported that the conflict between Kukis and Nagas flared after ethnic clashes between the Meitei and Kuki-Zo-Hmar communities began in May 2023. The Assembly was told in September that more than 300 people had been killed and 49 were missing since then. About 60,000 people were displaced, of whom 36,000 had been resettled and 24,000 remained in relief camps.
stories.whyItMatters: The leaders say a truce would bring immediate relief to affected families, and the Manipur conflict has displaced about 60,000 people, 24,000 of whom remain in relief camps.

stories.headline: Kilmar Ábrego García leaves US for Spain, ending deportation fight
stories.dek: The Salvadoran man, wrongly deported in 2025 and later returned, flew out on a commercial flight; the two sides describe his departure in sharply different terms.
stories.summary: Kilmar Ábrego García left the United States for Spain on Tuesday on a commercial flight, ending a legal fight over his removal. The Department of Homeland Security called it a self-deportation under a removal order; his lawyer called it temporary.
body: Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadoran man whose wrongful deportation in 2025 became a focal point in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration policy, left the United States for Spain on a commercial flight on Tuesday.

ABC News reported that its journalists saw him board a flight from a Washington, D.C.-area airport to Madrid. One of his attorneys confirmed he was bound for Spain, according to the Washington Post. The New York Times, citing his attorneys, reported that he ultimately plans to travel on to Mexico.

The terms of his departure have not been made public. CBS News reported that a federal judge overseeing his civil case in Maryland issued an order on Friday that remains sealed. Fox News, citing two sources familiar with the matter, reported that the judge ordered him to leave by Tuesday.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement: "We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain." He accused Ábrego García of being a human trafficker, wife beater, gang member and child predator. Ábrego García has denied the gang allegations, and the criminal case against him was dismissed.
DHS said on X that he left under a removal order, paid for his own flight, received no incentives under the voluntary departure programme, and "will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States."

Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat who visited Ábrego García in El Salvador in 2025, said in a statement that he was "travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."

His lawyer said in a statement that the departure was "temporary" and that he had "many options to return to the United States." The statement said: "We don't expect that to happen under this administration," but that the lawyers expect the next administration to prioritise reuniting the family and bringing him back to Maryland.
The BBC said it had contacted DHS for comment. Fox News said it had asked Ábrego García's attorney, the White House, DHS and Immigration and Customs Enforcement for comment.
keyFacts: Ábrego García flew to Spain on a commercial flight on Tuesday, November 24.
He was deported to El Salvador in March 2025 despite a court order barring it.
A federal judge dismissed his human smuggling case in May 2026 over a presumption of vindictive prosecution.
The administration had sought to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and Liberia; he had offered Costa Rica.
The judge's order tied to his departure remains sealed.
stories.background:
Ábrego García came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager and lived in Maryland with his wife, a US citizen. A 2019 immigration court order barred his removal to El Salvador because of the risk of gang persecution. He was deported there in March 2025, held in the Cecot prison, and returned in June 2025 after the Supreme Court ordered the government to facilitate his return. The administration called the deportation an administrative error.

He was then indicted on human smuggling charges over a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee and pleaded not guilty. Judge Waverly Crenshaw dismissed the case in May 2026; the Justice Department appealed, with Sixth Circuit arguments scheduled for February.
stories.whyItMatters: The departure ends months of litigation over where the administration could send him, though his lawyers say they will seek his return to the US and the Justice Department's appeal of the dismissal is pending.

stories.headline: Gunmen hold at least 20 hostages in Cartagena supermarket after failed cash raid
stories.dek: President Abelardo de la Espriella travelled to the city on Tuesday night as police, navy and special forces surrounded the Éxito store; no injuries have been reported.
stories.summary: Armed men have held at least 20 people inside an Éxito supermarket in Cartagena since Tuesday morning, after a failed attempt to rob an armoured cash vehicle. Ten hostages have been released, police said, and President Abelardo de la Espriella has arrived.
body: Armed men were holding at least 20 people hostage inside an Éxito supermarket in the Colombian tourist city of Cartagena on Tuesday night, hours after a failed attempt to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle, police and President Abelardo de la Espriella said.

About 30 people were initially seized early on Tuesday, according to police. By nightfall, 10 had been released, five of them elderly women. The Telegraph reported about 25 hostages; Al Jazeera and the South China Morning Post gave figures of around 20 and at least 20. No injuries have been reported so far.

The gunmen reportedly arrived at about 8.30am local time at the store in the La Castellana neighbourhood. De la Espriella said the group planned to rob an armoured vehicle due to collect the previous day's takings. Employees who saw the movement on security cameras alerted the national police, who surrounded the building, he said.

Customers are also believed to be among those held. Footage on social media showed dozens of people running out of the store, and local media showed snipers on nearby buildings. Reuters images showed a crowd of heavily armed military and police outside, and the Guardian reported scores of officers, navy personnel and special forces at the scene.

De la Espriella's motorcade reached Cartagena on Tuesday night, Agence France-Presse reported. The president is expected to take charge of the operation. Before travelling, he said the hostage-taking appeared to stem from a botched robbery by "common criminals" rather than an armed group.
Speaking in Villavicencio, he said the standoff "will turn out well for the hostages, but I'm not so sure it will turn out quite so well for the hostage-takers".
Jacob Perez, whose son works at the store, told AFP: "My son is there. He didn't leave work and he's not answering his phone. I think they took it from him."
The supermarket is about six miles from Cartagena's old city. The standoff was continuing late on Tuesday.
keyFacts: Gunmen seized about 30 people at an Éxito supermarket in Cartagena on Tuesday morning.
Ten hostages, including five elderly women, had been freed by nightfall, police said.
At least 20 people remain inside; outlets report figures from around 20 to 25.
The president said the group had planned to rob an armoured cash vehicle.
No injuries had been reported as of Tuesday night.
stories.background: The standoff followed several violent days in Colombia. A car bomb outside the Meta departmental government headquarters in Villavicencio on Monday night killed a security guard and injured more than 20 people; the president blamed a Farc dissident faction. In the early hours of Monday, drones believed to belong to the ELN dropped bombs in Cúcuta, injuring three civilians. De la Espriella has been in office for just over three months.
stories.whyItMatters: The lives of at least 20 customers and staff depend on the outcome, in a city that draws hundreds of thousands of visitors a year.

stories.headline: Eisenkot's Yashar signs first coalition pact with Lieberman's Our Home party
stories.dek: The former military chief, tasked by President Herzog with forming Israel's next government, has until December 6 to build a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
stories.summary: Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party said it signed a coalition pact with Avigdor Lieberman's Israel Our Home party, the first such deal since October's election. Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government, with an option to seek a 14-day extension.
body: Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party has signed a coalition agreement with Avigdor Lieberman's Israel Our Home party, the first such pact since Israel's October 27 election, as Eisenkot tries to form the next government.

Yashar said Eisenkot, a former military chief, met Lieberman and that the two leaders agreed on a deal afterwards. Al Jazeera reported that the parties agreed to sign the pact. NDTV reported that it had been signed.

No party won a 61-seat majority in the election. The Knesset was sworn in on November 10 without a new government in place. President Isaac Herzog has asked Eisenkot to form one, while Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister.

Eisenkot has until December 6 under the 28-day mandate. He could ask for a 14-day extension. If he fails, Netanyahu would get a turn, and if no one forms a coalition, another election would be held next year, NDTV reported.

Netanyahu's Likud and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies hold 53 of the Knesset's 120 seats, NDTV reported. That is short of a majority. Eisenkot's Yashar and its partners, including Lieberman, hold 48 seats. Yashar won 21 seats and Our Home won 7.
Parties representing Israel's Arab minority hold 19 seats and share Eisenkot's opposition to Netanyahu, NDTV reported.

NDTV described the deal as something of a surprise. Lieberman had been vocal in opposing a government that relies on Arab parties' support, and a unity government with Netanyahu. He has also said his main goal is to remove Netanyahu from power.

Talks continue between Eisenkot, some partners in his "change bloc" and Likud on a possible unity government. The left-wing Democrats party, which won 8 seats, said it was suspending talks with Eisenkot because of progress in those talks and the deadlock in negotiations on a "change government". Its leader, Yair Golan, has said he prefers a government without Netanyahu but with Arab parties.

stories.headline: Bangladesh raises garment workers' minimum wage 36% to 17,000 taka
stories.dek: A government-appointed wage board approved the new rate in a 4-2 vote after nearly 12 hours of talks, ending weeks of protests that shut factories.
stories.summary: Bangladesh's wage board raised the monthly minimum wage for garment workers by 36% to 17,000 taka ($139) on Wednesday. The increase, the smallest in more than a decade, takes effect on December 1 after weeks of protests.
body: Bangladesh raised the minimum monthly wage for garment workers by 36% to 17,000 taka ($139) on Wednesday, after weeks of protests by workers who had demanded higher pay.

A government-appointed wage board approved the new structure at around 2am after nearly 12 hours of talks between worker and employer representatives. Workers' representative Babul Akhter said the six-member board voted 4-2. Four members backed 17,000 taka and two backed the workers' demand for 18,000 taka.

The current minimum wage, set in 2023, is 12,500 taka. Under a four-grade structure, monthly pay will range from 17,000 taka for Grade 4 workers to 21,500 taka for Grade 1 workers. The new wages take effect on December 1, and workers are expected to receive the revised pay from January.

Board chairman Judge Syed Azad Subhani said the "majority supported a minimum wage of 17,000 taka". Workers first sought 32,000 taka, according to CNA and Mint, and lowered their demand to 18,000 taka during the talks. The Hindu reported an initial demand of 30,000 taka. Factory owners started at 15,000 taka and raised their offer to 17,000.

Akhter said workers' representatives urged people to return to factories after the deal. "Although we are not completely satisfied, the outcome is not entirely bad either," he told reporters. He added that workers previously received a revision every five years but this time got one after three.
The 36% rise is the smallest in more than a decade, following increases of 56% in 2023, 51% in 2018 and 77% in 2013, CNA and Mint reported, citing Reuters.

The protests, which began in October, shut factories, blocked highways and led to clashes with police, according to the reports. The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) said 397 factories could not operate on Tuesday and another 84 were closed under the labour law's "no work, no pay" provision.
A BGMEA survey estimated that 317 factories lost about $428 million in production over 18 days of disruption. Buyers shifted orders worth about $254 million to other countries, it said.

Factory owners have warned that further increases could raise production costs and weaken competitiveness. Labour rights groups say higher pay is needed to protect workers' living standards. CNA and Mint reported that the modest rise may not be enough to end the unrest.
keyFacts: The minimum wage rises 36% to 17,000 taka ($139) from 12,500 taka.
The wage board voted 4-2; two members backed 18,000 taka.
Monthly pay ranges from 17,000 taka (Grade 4) to 21,500 taka (Grade 1).
The new structure takes effect on December 1; workers expect revised pay from January.
BGMEA estimates $428 million in lost production and $254 million in orders shifted abroad.
stories.background: Bangladesh is the world's second-biggest garment exporter after China. The industry employs more than 4 million people, earns around $38 billion annually and accounts for more than 80% of export earnings. It supplies retailers including H&M, Zara, Walmart, Target and Gap. Workers say pay has not kept pace with the cost of food, housing, transport and health care.
stories.whyItMatters: The new rate affects more than 4 million garment workers in Bangladesh's main export industry. Employers say higher costs could hurt competitiveness, while workers say pay has lagged living costs.
